notes.decision: Translated as 'in your mouth, you yourself alone' — ⲣⲱⲕ ⲟⲩⲁⲉⲉⲧⲕ is the standard Coptic emphatic-reflexive idiom (cf. ⲣⲱ⸗ ⲟⲩⲁⲉⲉⲧ⸗) meaning 'thyself alone, by thy own self.' The leading [ⲍ] preposition specifies location: 'in your mouth' = i.e., the disciple's own utterance, contrasted with the truth itself. The Apostle is identifying the words as the disciple's private claim, not a teaching he has received from outside.

Translated 'which removes him from the suffering of the fasts.' The Lycopolitan ⲟⲩⲉⲓ̈ⲧϥ̄ likely combines ⲟⲩⲉⲓ 'be far/distant' (causative) + 3sg.m suffix = 'cause him to be far from.' The whole clause modifies ⲡⲉⲓ̈ 'this' (referring to the alleged 'nourishment'), reflecting the disciple's claim that some practice delivers from the suffering of fasting. Reading is moderate confidence; alternative readings (e.g., 'which they bring him') are possible but the 'remove from' sense fits best with following ⲛ̄ⲧⲗⲁⲓ̈ⲃⲉ 'from the suffering.'

Translated 'eager/willing' — qualitative of ⲣⲟⲟⲩⲧ 'be ready, prepared, joyful' (the standard Coptic verb of willingness/readiness). Modifies the 2sg subject in circumstantial: 'you being eager,' i.e., the disciple's eagerness in proclaiming his (mistaken) view.

Read ⲯⲱⲛⲉ as Lyc reflex of ⲡⲱⲱⲛⲉ 'turn aside, change' (with ⲯ for ⲡ in dialectal spelling), giving 'you did not turn aside from saying it.' Alternative: ⲯⲱⲛⲉ = ϣⲱⲛⲉ 'be sick, weary' giving 'you did not weary of saying it.' Both are contextually viable; chose 'turn aside' for stronger fit with the Apostle's accusation that the disciple boldly proclaimed his error.

Translated 'wasted' — apparent reduplicated qualitative of unidentified root, possibly cognate with ⲗⲁⲕⲗⲱⲕ 'soft, melt' (giving 'softened, weakened') or with a Lyc dialectal form for bodily decline. The triadic series 'wasted/sick/oppressed' marks progressive bodily failure; 'wasted' captures the cumulative-debilitation sense.

Read as Lyc reflex of ⲧⲁⲛϩⲟⲩⲧ 'entrust' + 2sg suffix = 'they have entrusted you.' With following ⲁⲣⲁϩ 'to it,' yields 'the work to which you have been entrusted.' This is the same construction underlying English passive 'entrusted to (a task).'

Translated 'your body is holy unto you' — ⲁⲩⲟⲛ̄ here is the Lycopolitan existential predicate (cf. accumulated entry ⲁⲩⲟ̄ⲛ 'exists / there belongs to him'). The qualitative ⲉϩⲟⲩⲁⲭ = ⲟⲩⲁⲁⲃ 'holy, pure' modifies ⲡⲉⲕⲥⲱⲙⲁ. The phrase belongs to what 'they shall say' to the disciple in the realm of rest — declaring that his bodily integrity has been preserved through fidelity to the work.

Translated 'harm' — lexeme of uncertain etymology, possibly Lycopolitan reflex of ϫⲃⲓⲛ 'lameness, deficiency' or related to ϭⲃⲃⲉ 'be weak.' Listed in the doublet/triplet with ⲧⲉⲕⲟ 'destruction' and ϯⲕⲉⲥ 'affliction' as the bodily ills from which the faithful disciple is preserved.

Translated 'this entire profit becomes worthless.' The form ⲛϯⲃⲁⲧ is obscure; tentatively read as ⲛ̄- (predicative/genitive) + ⲧⲃⲁⲧ from a root meaning 'spit, despise' (cf. Crum ⲧⲃⲏⲧ 'spittle/contempt'), yielding the predicate 'becomes-of-spittle' = 'becomes despised, becomes worthless.' Alternative readings (e.g., 'in vain,' 'lost') are possible. The argument requires the entire profit to be nullified if the work is refused.

Translated 'they do not give-heed-to ... the face of the profit.' Read ⲙⲁⲩⲧⲉ as Lycopolitan negative habitual ⲙⲁⲩ- + ⲧⲉ = 'they do not give' (the ⲧⲉ being a reduced infinitive of ϯ 'give'). With the restored object ⲡⲍⲟ ⲙ̄ⲡⲍⲏⲩ 'the face of the profit' (line 30), this yields the idiom ϯ-ϩⲟ ⲁ- 'give face/attention to,' standard Coptic for 'pay heed to, regard.' The Apostle's logic: even the wise (those most likely to grasp the truth) are not turning their face to the profit the disciple has been proclaiming, hence they will commit this sin (of refusal) along with him.

The lost word ending in -ⲓⲙⲟⲥ is most likely a Greek loanword. Plausible candidates include [ⲇⲟⲕ]ⲓⲙⲟⲥ 'approved, tested' (δόκιμος) or [ⲗⲟⲅ]ⲓⲙⲟⲥ 'reasonable, of repute' (λόγιμος). The sense 'wise men ... [approved/reasonable] who know the truth' fits the rhetorical structure but the specific term cannot be securely restored.

Translated 'this is the manner that I have' — the standard formulaic Apostle's self-assertion (cf. similar formulas elsewhere in the Kephalaia, e.g. K.193 'thus is the way'). The Apostle is contrasting his own constant teaching with the disciple's wavering. The sentence breaks at the page boundary; continuation would specify what 'I have' (taught/decreed/commanded).
